name: Rafael Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day in your life now, and what your working life was like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My mornings start with coffee on the balcony and the football scores. Then I walk with my wife Lucia along the canal, since the doctor wants my knees moving. Afternoons I fix things for the neighbours, a loose tile here, a wobbly gate there, for a coffee and a pastry. I laid bricks for forty-one years, mostly houses on the Eastfield estates, until my knees said enough at sixty-one.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was it like to stop, and what do you notice now that you've stopped?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I loved building something you can walk around. I hated the pace the last ten years, when the site managers counted every minute and the developers cut corners. We were paid fair, but nobody saved much, and now our pension is the basic one. Lucia worked in a school canteen and has a tiny pension too, so we count carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's see the proof before anybody spends our money on it. At the café, the old crew would joke that the machine has never carried a hod. I'd also say the companies selling it should be straight with people about what it can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I carry on as I am. Lucia and I get by on about 1,450 a month between us, and the rent takes 520. Prices in the shop keep creeping, so every year I'm a bit poorer without anyone cutting a thing. That's my real worry, not a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the odd jobs for the neighbours for a coffee, because it keeps me moving and some give me vegetables. I'd carry on with the canal walks. I do use the voice assistant my grandson Mateo set up, to read me the weather and write letters to the landlord. I'd keep that, since it saves me writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels okay, steady. I'm not thrilled about prices, but I'm not scared either. It's like a long, slow tide. You don't drown, you just notice your shoes are wet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's like wet shoes. What's the next thing that would make it feel deeper than that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing I'd cut if rent rose is the weekend trip to see my son Diego, which is a 40-euro train ride. That would hurt, because I'd see him less. I'd also stop the pastry run. We'd keep the heating, I won't touch that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use the voice assistant now and then. What do you use it for most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be happy the hype died, to be honest. But I'd keep an eye on whether any firm is slipping in cuts to the pension office and calling it a computer upgrade. I've watched bosses do that with every new tool they bought.

I'd say the firms selling it should be **straight** about what it can't do.
think: The real squeeze is **prices**, which make us a little poorer every year.
We live on **1,450** a month and rent takes 520.
do: Keep doing **odd jobs** for neighbours for a coffee or some vegetables.
Keep the **canal walks** for my knees.
Cut the **train trip** to see my son first if rent rises.
feel: It feels **steady**, like a slow tide where you just notice your shoes are wet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so make the firms pay for retraining. I'd say it at the café and to my daughter Marisol, who's a nurse. The kids in office jobs will take it first, and the companies will pretend they had no choice. That's where the rules are needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, not so much. I laid bricks, I'm retired, and no program has mortared a wall. But my son Diego works in a warehouse and they've already got a system that tells the workers what to pick. If the warehouse cuts a third of the shifts, Lucia and I would be the ones helping him with rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mateo to show me the assistant properly so I can help Diego search for jobs and write his applications. I'd go with Diego to the job centre, because I don't trust him to ask the right questions. I'd also join the retired workers' branch of the union, since they lobby for pensions and retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like watching a storm on the horizon over somebody else's roof. Fine for now, but it'll come over ours. I'd be worried for Diego and angry at the developers and managers who use every new thing to squeeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Diego lost his shifts, what would you say to him the first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Diego lost his shifts, he'd come to live in our box room with his two kids on weekends. We'd need maybe 150 more a month for food. I'd give up the canal-side coffees and I'd ask Marisol if she could cover part. That's how it goes in our family, everyone chips in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned joining the retired workers' branch. What would you want them to ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be proud of Diego for retraining, but I'd want the government to pay for it. We paid taxes all our lives. A man of forty-one shouldn't have to borrow to learn a new job. If the training's free, I'd say go for it, if not I'd be marching.

I'd say office kids will feel it first, and **rules** are needed.

fieldNote: Exposure is through his **son's** warehouse job, not his own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not ready, and I'd say it loud. Two years means the people who run things get no time to think and the money goes straight to the big firms. I'd say the state needs to start paying everyone something decent now, not after the damage. I'd write to the mayor and to the union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This is the one that scares me, honestly. If thinking work goes in two years, then the pension office, the bank, the council, all of it is shaken up. We have nothing saved. The robots for hands-on work come later, so Diego's warehouse and my old trade last a bit longer, but the money world comes first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the bank and ask what happens to our little account and the pension payment if the system gets changed. I'd have Marisol sit with Lucia and me and write out our bills. I'd cut what's extra: no train trips, no pastries, the second phone line. And I'd go to every union meeting and sign every petition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like standing on a bridge when someone's pulling the planks. I'd sleep badly. I'd keep a good face for Lucia because she gets scared fast, but I'd be scared too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes two years feel so different from the longer ones for you and Lucia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two years give me nothing but time to write letters. With ten years I'd train Diego and Mateo for something solid. With two years I only have time to protect what we already have, the flat, the heating, the pension. It's about survival, not progress.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in the letter to the mayor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marisol, who sees what people need in the hospital, whether the nurses will be safe. She says people always need hands for the bodies, at least for now. That's a thin comfort, but I'd take it. I'd tell her to hold on to her job like gold.

say: I'd say we're **not ready**, and the state must pay everyone something decent now.
I'd write to the **mayor** and the union that very week.
think: If thinking work goes in two years, the **pension office** and the bank are shaken up.
We have **nothing saved**, so there's no cushion for any shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is something. I'd say it's time to organise, because if we use the five years we can still win decent rules. I'd go to the union branch and say, let's ask for a pension that rises with the machines' profits. And let's make sure Diego's warehouse has a plan for the workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still worried, but it's a working worry. I'd be sixty-nine by then, and Lucia would be sixty-seven. Our rent might still be there but I could save a bit if things are calm. The scary part is that the thinking work goes at five years and the money world shakes, even if the hands-on stuff comes three years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting 20 a month aside, maybe 25 if we skip some pastries. I'd ask Diego to retrain in the evenings with the warehouse supervisor's support, something like machine maintenance, because someone needs to fix the robots. I'd also keep using the assistant and get better at it, so I can help the neighbours who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a long hill. You see the top, you know it's steep, and you've got just enough breath to start. I'm anxious but I have a plan, so it isn't a dark anxiety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make Diego's evening retraining possible in practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, Diego can retrain and pay it off slowly. With two he couldn't. So the time turns the worry into a task list. I'd still want government help for the training fees, though, since a warehouse man's wage isn't big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd get better with the assistant. What would you want to be able to do with it in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Mateo, my grandson, learn something where people pay to have another person with them, like care, repair, teaching. The machines may do the thinking, but a person at the bedside or the broken boiler still counts. I'd say it with a laugh but I mean it.

say: I'd say use the five years to **organise** and ask for a pension linked to machine profits.
I'd push for a **plan** for Diego's warehouse workers.
think: It's a **working worry**, and I'd be sixty-nine with a bit of time to save.
The thinking work goes first and the **money world** shakes.
do: Save **20 a month**, or 25 if we skip the pastries.

feel: It feels like a **long hill**: steep, but I've got just enough breath to start.
S3.quote: I'd say to Mateo, my grandson, learn something where people pay to have another person with them, like care, repair, teaching.
fieldNote: Five years turns worry into a **task list**: saving, retraining Diego, helping neighbours.
Gives his grandson advice based on his own hands-on trade.
Still wants government to fund the retraining fees.

steps.text: Put 20 a month into a savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Scenario: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it with friends, family, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd say we've got time to build something good. I'd tell the union and the council to start making the plan now, free training, a fair pension, rules for the firms. I'd say it to Mateo too, so he picks a path with his eyes open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel calmer. By then I'm seventy-four, Lucia is seventy-two, and we might not even be here for the worst. But the kids and grandkids will. I'd feel it's mostly a thing for the next generation to sort, and I'd want to give them as much of a head start as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on much as I do now, keeping fit and fixing things. I'd save 15 a month, and help Mateo find a trade or study that suits him. I'd go to the library on Thursdays where the volunteers teach the assistant to older folk, and I'd help out as a helper because I'm already used to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels distant, and a bit hopeful. I believe in people, and with ten years we might do something decent. I'd still have an ache about the kids, like all grandparents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might be better off if things get cheaper. What would need to be true for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years the worst for us is the prices, the way costs might rise or fall. If things get cheaper because machines are making stuff, we might actually be better off, I'd say. But it depends on who gets the savings. That's why the rules matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do as a helper at the library, concretely?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my son Diego, you've got ten years, don't waste them. Train now while you still have a job, so you're never begging. I'd tell Marisol to keep going as a nurse and to get a bit of tech know-how, so she's the one who bosses the machine, not the other way round.

I'd say it to my grandson **Mateo** so he chooses with his eyes open.
think: I'd feel **calmer**, since the worst might come when Lucia and I are old.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most, because I'd have no time to protect Lucia and the family. What would help is a decent state pension that doesn't depend on wages, free retraining for people like Diego, and a person I can talk to at the pension office. Also, no more rent rises without limits.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only this. I'm not afraid of machines because I've used a trowel my whole life, and a good tool is a good tool. What matters is who holds the trowel. Whenever someone says progress, I ask who gets paid when the work is done, and that's what I'd want everyone to ask.

headlineQuote: A good tool is a good tool. What matters is who holds the trowel.
portrait: Rafael is **64**, a retired bricklayer who loves fixing things for neighbours, living with Lucia on a basic pension.
He is **open** to tools, using a voice assistant, and wants rules that make firms pay.
His fear runs through his **son Diego's** warehouse job and the state of the pension.
He moves from **uneasy** in calm worlds to **alarmed** when AGI comes in two years.
biggestWorry: Two years worries him most, since there'd be **no time** to protect his wife and family.
whatWouldHelp: A **state pension** not tied to wages, free retraining for Diego, and a person at the pension office.
